etymology: From Old French percer, to bore through. Webster 1828: penetrated; entered by force; transfixed. In Scripture it is the word of the crucifixion prophesied a thousand years and five hundred years before it happened, and the word John chose to prove that the prophecy had been kept in the flesh.
biblical_def: Pierced is the crucifixion word. David wrote it in the psalm of the cross, centuries before the Romans invented the punishment: For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet (Psalm 22:16). Zechariah put it in the mouth of the LORD Himself, in the first person, and joined it to a promise of repentance: they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son (Zechariah 12:10). John, standing at the cross and watching a soldier open the side of Jesus with a spear, records that he saw it and bore record that ye might believe, and then cites the prophet: They shall look on him whom they pierced (John 19:37). The pronouns in Zechariah are the ones the Socinian and the modern liberal cannot handle — they shall look upon me, and then they shall mourn for him — God pierced, and the pierced One mourned for as another Person. Paul takes the same verb for a self-inflicted wound: those who covet after money have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows (1 Timothy 6:10).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PIERCE as to thrust into with a pointed instrument; to penetrate; to enter; and figuratively, to affect deeply, as to pierce the heart with grief. Both the literal and the affective senses are at work in Zechariah 12:10 and Luke 2:35.
webster_full: PIERCE, v.t. — To thrust into with a pointed instrument; to penetrate; to stab.
To enter; to force a way into; as, the shot pierced the wall.
To affect deeply; to penetrate the heart with grief or with conviction; as, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also (Luke 2:35).
PIERCED, pp. — Penetrated; transfixed; deeply affected.
The word of Acts 2:37, they were pricked in their heart, renders a different Greek verb but the same figure — the word of God entering like a point.
scriptures: Psalm 22:16
For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet.
Zechariah 12:10

And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn.
John 19:37
And again another scripture saith, They shall look on him whom they pierced.
Isaiah 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
1 Timothy 6:10
For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
corruption_summary: Psalm 22:16 is the most contested verse in Old Testament textual history, and the modern habit of dismissing the Christian reading as a pious alteration misstates the evidence and misses what the psalm as a whole is doing.
corruption_paragraphs: The Masoretic tradition at Psalm 22:16 reads a form usually rendered like a lion; the Septuagint, translated by Jews centuries before Christ, reads a verb meaning they pierced, and the Syriac and other ancient witnesses agree. A Hebrew manuscript from Nahal Hever supports the verbal reading as well. The Authorized Version follows the older and better-attested tradition, and the psalm around it settles the matter for any honest reader: bones out of joint, the tongue cleaving to the jaws, garments parted and lots cast for the vesture, and the cry with which our Lord opened the whole psalm from the cross. Whatever one concludes about the consonants, this is a description of a crucifixion written by a man who had never seen one.

Zechariah 12:10 is the harder text for anti-Trinitarian readings, and it should be pressed. The speaker who pours out the spirit of grace and supplications is the LORD, and He says they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and in the next clause the mourning is for him. One divine speaker, pierced, and mourned for as a distinct Person. John quotes it of the spear-thrust and Revelation 1:7 quotes it of the second advent. The doctrine of the Trinity is not a later imposition upon the Hebrew Scriptures; the Hebrew Scriptures contain sentences that cannot be construed without it, and this is one of them.
roots_summary: Hebrew karah or ka’ari at Psalm 22:16, and daqar (H1856), to pierce or thrust through, at Zechariah 12:10; Greek ekkenteo (G1574) in John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7.
roots_lines: Hebrew daqar (H1856) — to pierce, to thrust through; Zechariah 12:10, and of the fatal thrust in 1 Samuel 31:4.
Greek ekkenteo (G1574) — to pierce, to prick out; John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7, both quoting Zechariah.
Greek nusso (G3572) — to prick, to pierce; the soldier’s spear in John 19:34.
Greek peripeiro (G4044) — to pierce through, to impale on a spit; pierced themselves through with many sorrows (1 Timothy 6:10).
Greek rhomphaia (G4501) — a large broadsword; the sword Simeon said would pierce Mary’s own soul (Luke 2:35).
usage: They pierced my hands and my feet (Psalm 22:16) — a crucifixion described a thousand years before the Romans devised it.
They shall look upon me whom they have pierced (Zechariah 12:10) — the LORD speaking of His own piercing.
Pierced themselves through with many sorrows (1 Timothy 6:10) — the self-inflicted wound of covetousness.

etymology: From Latin provocare, to call forth, to challenge. Webster 1828: the act of provoking; anything that excites anger. In Scripture the provocation, with the article, is a proper name for one place and one day — Meribah, where Israel tempted God at the rock, and which Hebrews makes the standing warning to the church.
biblical_def: The provocation is a technical term. Psalm 95 gives it: Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, and as in the day of temptation in the wilderness (Psalm 95:8), where the Hebrew has the place-names Meribah and Massah — strife and testing — the water from the rock at Rephidim and again at Kadesh. The writer to the Hebrews takes that psalm and preaches it twice to Christians: Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness (Hebrews 3:8), and again at Hebrews 3:15, with the whole warning of chapters 3 and 4 built on it. The offence is stated by God Himself as unbelief in the face of evidence: How long will this people provoke me? and how long will it be ere they believe me, for all the signs which I have shewed among them? (Numbers 14:11). That is the anatomy of provocation. It is not the sin of a man who has seen nothing; it is the sin of a people who came through the sea, ate the manna daily, and still asked whether God was among them. Hebrews draws the application without softening it: those bodies fell in the wilderness, and they could not enter in because of unbelief.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PROVOCATION as the act of provoking; anything that excites anger; and, in law, an appeal to a higher court. The Latin root means to call forth or summon — provocation calls anger out of the one provoked.
webster_full: PROVOCATION, n. — The act of provoking; anything that excites anger or resentment.
The cause of resentment; that which stirs up displeasure.
In law, an appeal to a superior court — the original Latin sense of calling forth.
In Scripture, the provocation with the definite article denotes the events at Meribah and Massah (Exodus 17; Numbers 20).
The Hebrew place-names carry the meaning: Meribah is strife or chiding, and Massah is temptation or testing.
scriptures: Psalm 95:8
Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, and as in the day of temptation in the wilderness:
Hebrews 3:8
Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness:
Hebrews 3:15
While it is said, To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts, as in the provocation.
Numbers 14:11
And the LORD said unto Moses, How long will this people provoke me? and how long will it be ere they believe me, for all the signs which I have shewed among them?
Isaiah 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
corruption_summary: Hebrews 3 and 4 are the classic Arminian proof texts for the loss of salvation, and the classic ground of easy-believism’s embarrassment; the Reformed reading takes the warning at full strength precisely because perseverance is a doctrine about the means God uses.
corruption_paragraphs: The warning is real, and any exposition that blunts it has failed. Take heed, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God. The Reformed answer is not that the warning is hypothetical but that warnings are among the means by which God keeps His own. The same chapter that says the elect cannot finally fall also says exhort one another daily, while it is called To day — and the exhortation is the instrument. A man who hears Hebrews 3, is alarmed, and holds fast is exhibiting the perseverance the doctrine describes; a man who hears it, shrugs, and hardens is showing what he always was. The wilderness generation is the standing case: they had every external privilege of the covenant and no faith, and Hebrews says the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it.

The opposite abuse is the easy-believism that treats the warning as irrelevant to anyone who once made a decision. Numbers 14:11 exposes it. God’s complaint is not that Israel had never professed; it is that after the plagues, the sea, the pillar, and the manna they still would not believe Him. Repeated exposure to God’s works without trust does not produce neutrality. It produces hardness, and hardness is cumulative — which is why the text says To day three times. The provocation was not one bad afternoon. It was ten temptings, and the sentence when it fell was forty years long.
roots_summary: Hebrew Meribah (H4809), strife, and Massah (H4532), temptation — the place-names Psalm 95:8 uses; Greek parapikrasmos (G3894), a bitter provocation, in Hebrews 3.
roots_lines: Hebrew Meribah (H4809) — strife, chiding; the place named at Exodus 17:7 and Numbers 20:13.
Hebrew Massah (H4532) — temptation, testing; the companion name at Exodus 17:7.
Hebrew na’ats (H5006) — to spurn, to provoke, to despise; how long will this people provoke me? (Numbers 14:11).
Greek parapikrasmos (G3894) — provocation, embitterment; Hebrews 3:8, 15, occurring nowhere else in the New Testament.
Greek skleruno (G4645) — to harden; harden not your hearts, the same verb used of Pharaoh in the Septuagint.
usage: Harden not your heart, as in the provocation (Psalm 95:8) — Meribah made a permanent warning.
How long will it be ere they believe me? (Numbers 14:11) — God’s own diagnosis of the offence.
As in the provocation (Hebrews 3:15) — the wilderness preached to the church, twice in one chapter.

etymology: From Old English hore. The Authorized Version’s idiom is to go a whoring after, rendering a Hebrew verb for harlotry used figuratively of idolatry. The translators chose the coarse word deliberately, because God had chosen the coarse figure deliberately.
biblical_def: Whoring is the Authorized Version’s rendering of God’s own metaphor for idolatry, and He uses it without apology. The covenant at Sinai is a marriage, and the worship of another god is therefore adultery, not a difference of religious opinion. The warning is issued before Israel enters the land: lest thou make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and they go a whoring after their gods… And thou take of their daughters unto thy sons, and their daughters go a whoring after their gods, and make thy sons go a whoring after their gods (Exodus 34:15-16). The book of Judges records the outcome in a single sentence: they would not hearken unto their judges, but they went a whoring after other gods (Judges 2:17). Even a good man’s well-meant relic can become the object — Gideon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house (Judges 8:27). And the psalm turns the figure inward, past foreign gods altogether: they were defiled with their own works, and went a whoring with their own inventions (Psalm 106:39). Idolatry does not require a foreign shrine. A man’s own inventions will serve.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WHOREDOM in its scriptural sense as idolatry, the desertion of the worship of the true God for the worship of idols — noting the figurative use directly. The English coarseness is the point: God is describing a betrayal of the most intimate covenant.
webster_full: WHORING, ppr. — In Scripture, following after idols; committing spiritual fornication.
WHOREDOM, n. — In Scripture, idolatry; the desertion of the worship of the true God, for the worship of idols.
Webster records the figurative sense as a proper scriptural definition, not as a curiosity — the usage was familiar to every reader of the Authorized Version.
The idiom to go a whoring after preserves an old English construction with the prefixed particle, as in a-hunting and a-fishing.
Hosea is the sustained working out of the figure, with the prophet’s own marriage as the living parable.
scriptures: Exodus 34:15
Lest thou make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and they go a whoring after their gods, and do sacrifice unto their gods, and one call thee, and thou eat of his sacrifice;
Judges 2:17

And yet they would not hearken unto their judges, but they went a whoring after other gods, and bowed themselves unto them: they turned quickly out of the way which their fathers walked in, obeying the commandments of the LORD; but they did not so.
Judges 8:27
And Gideon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house.
Psalm 106:39
Thus were they defiled with their own works, and went a whoring with their own inventions.
1 Chronicles 5:25
And they transgressed against the God of their fathers, and went a whoring after the gods of the people of the land, whom God destroyed before them.
corruption_summary: The metaphor itself is now the offence. Modern readers object to God’s language as demeaning, and modern translations often soften it — which removes precisely the covenantal shock the figure was given to produce.
corruption_paragraphs: Feminist and progressive readings of Hosea and Ezekiel 16 and 23 charge the prophets with degrading imagery, and some evangelical commentators have begun to apologize for the texts rather than expound them. The objection misreads who is being indicted. In every case the unfaithful wife is the covenant people as a whole — priests, elders, kings, and congregation, overwhelmingly men — and the figure is chosen because marriage is the closest and most binding of human bonds and its betrayal the most wounding. God does not say Israel broke a rule. He says she broke a marriage. Soften the figure and you have softened the doctrine of the covenant, and with it the doctrine of grace, because the astonishing thing in Hosea is that the husband buys her back.

The subtler corruption is the assumption that idolatry requires an idol. Psalm 106:39 forecloses it: they went a whoring with their own inventions. Gideon’s ephod was made from the spoil of a victory God had given, by a man who had just refused the crown, and it became a snare to him and to his house. Calvin’s judgment that the human heart is a perpetual factory of idols is exactly this verse in a phrase. The question for a modern congregation is not whether it keeps a shrine but what it cannot be parted from, what it consults first, and what it would not surrender if God asked.
roots_summary: Hebrew zanah (H2181), to commit fornication, used figuratively of idolatry throughout; the noun zenunim (H2183), whoredoms, and taznuth (H8457) in Ezekiel.
roots_lines: Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to commit harlotry; the verb behind go a whoring after in every instance.
Hebrew zenunim (H2183) — whoredoms; Hosea 1:2, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms.
Hebrew na’aph (H5003) — to commit adultery; the companion figure, used of the covenant breach in Jeremiah 3:8.
Hebrew ephod (H646) — the priestly garment; Gideon’s became the object of Israel’s whoredom (Judges 8:27).
Greek porneia (G4202) — fornication; carried into Revelation 17 of the great harlot and her wine.
usage: They go a whoring after their gods (Exodus 34:15) — the warning issued before the land was entered.
All Israel went thither a whoring after it (Judges 8:27) — a good man’s ephod becoming a snare.
Went a whoring with their own inventions (Psalm 106:39) — idolatry needing no foreign shrine.

etymology: From Late Latin bassus, low, through Old French. Webster 1828: low in place, in value, in station, or in estimation; mean; vile. The adjective is entirely distinct from the noun meaning a foundation, and the Authorized Version uses the adjective of what God chooses and of what Paul’s critics called him.
biblical_def: Base in the Authorized Version means low, of no account, despised. Paul makes it the hinge of the argument that governs the whole doctrine of calling: base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are (1 Corinthians 1:28). The stated purpose follows immediately — that no flesh should glory in his presence. God’s election of the low is not sentiment about the poor; it is a deliberate strategy against boasting, of a piece with reducing Gideon’s army to three hundred. Paul then reports the word being thrown at him: I Paul myself beseech you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, who in presence am base among you, but being absent am bold toward you (2 Corinthians 10:1). The Corinthians thought his bodily presence weak and his speech contemptible, and he answers by appealing to the meekness of Christ rather than by asserting himself. Malachi shows the other direction — God makes men base for their partiality: therefore have I also made you contemptible and base before all the people, according as ye have not kept my ways, but have been partial in the law (Malachi 2:9). What God exalts and what He abases are both His own doing.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BASE, a. as low in place; of humble birth or station; mean-spirited; of little comparative value, as base metal; and illegitimate, as base-born. The 1828 senses of low station and low character were still distinguishable, as they are in Scripture.
webster_full: BASE, a. — Low in place; of humble birth, degree or station; mean; vile; worthless.
Of little comparative value; applied to metals, as base coin, and to any inferior sort.
Deep or grave in sound, as a base voice — a spelling since separated as bass.
Illegitimate; born out of wedlock, as base-born.
The noun BASE, a foundation or pedestal, is from Greek basis and is an entirely different word; the two must not be confused in reading 1 Corinthians 1:28.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 1:28
And base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are:
2 Corinthians 10:1
Now I Paul myself beseech you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, who in presence am base among you, but being absent am bold toward you:
Malachi 2:9
Therefore have I also made you contemptible and base before all the people, according as ye have not kept my ways, but have been partial in the law.
Psalm 8:4
What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?
Philippians 3:21
Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself.
corruption_summary: 1 Corinthians 1:28 is regularly recruited for liberation readings that make the poor the subject of salvation rather than its recipients, and it is equally abused by a respectability religion that quietly builds churches around the influential.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberation theology reads God’s choice of the base as a preferential option that makes the poor the hermeneutical key and the agents of their own deliverance. Paul’s stated reason will not carry it. God chose the foolish, the weak, the base, and the things which are not that no flesh should glory in his presence — the purpose is the abolition of boasting, not the elevation of a class. Poverty saves no one; the same chapter says of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption. The verse humbles the rich without flattering the poor, which is exactly what the gospel always does.

The opposite corruption is more common in comfortable churches and rarely says its name. It is the instinct to build a ministry around the impressive convert, the notable athlete, the man of influence — on the reasoning that God can use such a person more widely. Paul says God’s method is the reverse, and He gave the reason. James forbids the practice outright: the man with the gold ring and goodly apparel and the poor man in vile raiment are not to be seated differently, and to do so is to be judges of evil thoughts. A congregation can tell what it believes about 1 Corinthians 1:28 by who it defers to.
roots_summary: Greek agenes (G36), of no family, base-born, low; tapeinos (G5011), lowly, humble, in 2 Corinthians 10:1; Hebrew shaphal (H8217), low, in Malachi 2:9.
roots_lines: Greek agenes (G36) — without family, of no birth, base; a hapax legomenon at 1 Corinthians 1:28.
Greek tapeinos (G5011) — low, humble, of no account; in presence am base among you (2 Corinthians 10:1).
Greek exoutheneo (G1848) — to despise, to make of no account; things which are despised in the same verse.
Hebrew shaphal (H8217) — low, humble, base; Malachi 2:9, and Isaiah 57:15 of the God who dwells with the humble.
The English adjective is from Late Latin bassus, low; the unrelated noun is from Greek basis, a stepping or foundation.
usage: Base things of the world… hath God chosen (1 Corinthians 1:28) — election aimed at the abolition of boasting.
In presence am base among you (2 Corinthians 10:1) — the Corinthians’ estimate of an apostle.
Made you contemptible and base before all the people (Malachi 2:9) — God abasing partial priests.

etymology: From Greek astron, a star, and logos, word or reckoning. Webster 1828 distinguishes astrology, the pretended art of foretelling events by the stars, from astronomy, the science of the heavens. In Daniel and Isaiah the astrologers are the professional wise men of Babylon, and they are always exhibited failing.
biblical_def: The astrologers in Scripture are a class of Babylonian court professionals, named with the magicians, the sorcerers, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers, and the narrative purpose of every appearance is the same. Nebuchadnezzar commanded to call the magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans, for to shew the king his dreams (Daniel 2:2), and they could not, because he would not tell them the dream. Daniel states the conclusion for the record: The secret which the king hath demanded cannot the wise men, the astrologers, the magicians, the soothsayers, shew unto the king; But there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets (Daniel 2:27-28). At Belshazzar’s feast the same guild is summoned to read four words on a wall and cannot (Daniel 5:7). Isaiah’s taunt over Babylon is the definitive verdict: Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee (Isaiah 47:13) — and the next verse says they shall be as stubble the fire burns. The law had already put the whole trade under the ban: there shall not be found among you an observer of times, an enchanter, a witch, or a consulter with familiar spirits.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ASTROLOGY as the pretended science of foretelling future events by the aspects and positions of the heavenly bodies, and notes that it was formerly divided into natural and judiciary — the latter being the divination Scripture forbids.
webster_full: ASTROLOGER, n. — One who professes to foretell future events by the aspects and situation of the stars.
ASTROLOGY, n. — A pretended science which teaches to judge of the effects and influences of the stars, and to foretell future events.
Webster distinguishes natural astrology — the calculation of eclipses and tides, which is astronomy — from judiciary astrology, the divination of human affairs.
The Chaldeans were so identified with the practice that Chaldean became a synonym for astrologer in classical and later English usage.
Webster’s word pretended is the right one: the objection is not merely that the practice is forbidden but that it does not work.
scriptures: Daniel 2:2
Then the king commanded to call the magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans, for to shew the king his dreams. So they came and stood before the king.
Daniel 2:27
Daniel answered in the presence of the king, and said, The secret which the king hath demanded cannot the wise men, the astrologers, the magicians, the soothsayers, shew unto the king;
Daniel 5:7

The king cried aloud to bring in the astrologers, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers. And the king spake, and said to the wise men of Babylon, Whosoever shall read this writing, and shew me the interpretation thereof, shall be clothed with scarlet, and have a chain of gold about his neck, and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom.
Isaiah 47:13
Thou art wearied in the multitude of thy counsels. Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee.
Jeremiah 10:2
Thus saith the LORD, Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven; for the heathen are dismayed at them.
corruption_summary: Astrology is now treated as harmless entertainment, and horoscopes appear in publications that would never print a prayer — which is exactly the condition in which a forbidden practice does its quietest work.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 18 puts divination, observing times, enchantment, witchcraft, and consulting familiar spirits in one list and calls them all an abomination, and then gives the alternative in the same passage: God will raise up a Prophet, and to Him ye shall hearken. That is the structure of the whole biblical argument. Divination is forbidden not merely because it is false but because it is a rival channel of guidance, an attempt to get the future without getting it from God. Modern astrology’s claim to be a bit of fun does not change the category; it changes only the seriousness with which the practitioner holds it, and Jeremiah’s be not dismayed at the signs of heaven is addressed precisely to people who half believed.

There is a second and more respectable form of the same instinct, and Christians fall into it constantly: the search for a technique that will yield the will of God without the ordinary means. Fleeces, impressions treated as revelation, opening the Bible at random, and the endless hunt for a personal word are the church’s own prognostication. The Reformed answer is unglamorous and sufficient. God has spoken in the Scriptures, He gives wisdom to them that ask, He governs providence entirely, and the secret things belong unto Him. Daniel’s answer to Nebuchadnezzar is the whole doctrine in a sentence: there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets — and He does it when and as He pleases, to those who pray.
roots_summary: Aramaic ashshaph (H825), an enchanter or astrologer, in Daniel; Hebrew chabar shamayim, dividers of the heavens, in Isaiah 47:13; Greek astron plus logos for the English word.
roots_lines: Aramaic ashshaph (H825) — conjurer, enchanter, astrologer; Daniel 2:2, 2:27, 5:7, 5:11.
Hebrew hobre shamayim — dividers or observers of the heavens; the Authorized Version’s astrologers at Isaiah 47:13.
Hebrew chozim bakkokabim — stargazers, those who gaze at the stars; the parallel phrase in the same verse.
Hebrew qasam (H7080) — to practise divination; the general term forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10.
Hebrew anan (H6049) — to observe times, to practise soothsaying; the second item in the same prohibition.
usage: The magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans (Daniel 2:2) — the guild summoned and defeated.
Let now the astrologers, the stargazers… stand up, and save thee (Isaiah 47:13) — the prophet’s taunt over Babylon.
Learn not the way of the heathen (Jeremiah 10:2) — the command that covers every form of it.

etymology: From Old English heawan, to cut or strike with an edged tool. Webster 1828: one who cuts wood or stone. In Scripture the hewers are the lowest rank of the labour force, and the phrase hewers of wood and drawers of water has passed from Joshua 9 into English as the standing name for the humblest work.
biblical_def: The hewers enter Scripture through the Gibeonites’ deceit. Having tricked Israel into a league with mouldy bread and clouted shoes, they were found out, and Joshua could not break an oath sworn by the LORD. So the princes ruled: Let them live; but let them be hewers of wood and drawers of water unto all the congregation (Joshua 9:21). Joshua added the detail that turned the sentence into a mercy: it was for the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD, even unto this day, in the place which he should choose (Joshua 9:27). A people under the ban became servants of the sanctuary and lived beside the altar for centuries; they are still there in Nehemiah’s day as the Nethinim. Solomon set fourscore thousand hewers in the mountain for the temple (2 Chronicles 2:18). The word turns dark only once, and it is the greatest of the prophetic indictments: my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water (Jeremiah 2:13). There the hewing is man’s own labour to secure what God was already giving freely, and every stroke of the chisel was wasted.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HEWER as one who hews wood or stone, and HEW as to cut with an axe or other instrument, and to form or shape with a cutting tool. The scriptural phrase hewers of wood and drawers of water he treats as proverbial for the meanest service.
webster_full: HEWER, n. — One who hews wood or stone.
HEW, v.t. — To cut with an axe or other sharp instrument; to chop; to fell.
To form or shape with a cutting instrument; as, to hew a stone, to hew out a sepulchre.
Hewers of wood and drawers of water — proverbially, those who perform the meanest offices; from Joshua 9:21.
Deuteronomy 29:11 shows the phrase was already a settled expression for the lowest station within the covenant assembly.
scriptures: Joshua 9:21
And the princes said unto them, Let them live; but let them be hewers of wood and drawers of water unto all the congregation; as the princes had promised them.
Joshua 9:27
And Joshua made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD, even unto this day, in the place which he should choose.
2 Chronicles 2:18
And he set threescore and ten thousand of them to be bearers of burdens, and fourscore thousand to be hewers in the mountain, and three thousand and six hundred overseers to set the people a work.
Jeremiah 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
Deuteronomy 29:11
Your little ones, your wives, and thy stranger that is in thy camp, from the hewer of thy wood unto the drawer of thy water:
corruption_summary: Jeremiah 2:13 is the definitive statement of what every false religion and every self-made righteousness actually is: not the rejection of water, but the substitution of hard, cracked, self-quarried tanks for a living spring.
corruption_paragraphs: Two evils, and the prophet numbers them. The first is forsaking the fountain of living waters — a spring that runs without being worked, that costs nothing, that is simply there. The second is the labour of hewing cisterns out of rock, which in Judah’s limestone required weeks of chiselling and then plastering, and which cracked and lost the water anyway. That is the anatomy of works-righteousness, and it explains why it is so hard to abandon: the cistern represents effort, and a man will not easily walk away from something he has cut out of stone with his own hands. Every system of religion that requires a man to produce his own standing before God is a cistern, and Jeremiah’s point is that they all leak.

The Gibeonite sentence teaches the complementary lesson, and it is a gentler one. They lied to save their lives and were sentenced to perpetual menial service, and the sentence put them beside the altar of the LORD for the rest of Israel’s history. Centuries later, when Saul slew them in his zeal, God sent a three-year famine on Israel for it (2 Samuel 21:1) — the Judge of all the earth defending a people who had entered the covenant by fraud, because Israel had sworn. God keeps oaths sworn in His name even when the swearing was foolish, and He has a habit of making the lowest place in His house better than the highest place outside it. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
roots_summary: Hebrew chatab (H2404), to cut or gather wood, whence hewers of wood; chatsab (H2672), to hew or quarry stone, the verb of Jeremiah 2:13.
roots_lines: Hebrew chatab (H2404) — to cut wood, to gather firewood; hewers of wood (Joshua 9:21).
Hebrew chatsab (H2672) — to hew, to quarry, to dig out; hewed them out cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13).
Hebrew bor (H953) — a cistern, a pit; the hewn tank that will not hold water.
Hebrew mayim chayyim — living waters, that is, running spring water as opposed to stored water.
Hebrew Nethinim (H5411) — the given ones; the temple servants of Ezra and Nehemiah, traditionally traced to the Gibeonites.
usage: Let them be hewers of wood and drawers of water (Joshua 9:21) — a sentence that became a place beside the altar.
Fourscore thousand to be hewers in the mountain (2 Chronicles 2:18) — the labour behind the temple’s stone.
Hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13) — the exhausting industry of works-righteousness.

etymology: From Latin labor, toil; the Authorized Version keeps the British spelling with the u. Webster 1828: one who labours in a toilsome occupation; a man who does work that requires little skill, as distinguished from an artisan. In the Gospels it is the word for the men the Lord of the harvest sends out.
biblical_def: Labourers is our Lord’s own word for gospel ministers, and He chose a harvest-field word rather than a temple word. Seeing the multitudes scattered abroad as sheep having no shepherd, he was moved with compassion on them, and then said: The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few; Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest (Matthew 9:37-38). Three things are fixed by that command. The harvest is His, the labourers are His to send, and the church’s appointed part in the shortage is prayer. The very next chapter sends the twelve, so the men who prayed became the answer. The parable of the vineyard uses the same word for those hired at every hour, including the eleventh, and the householder pays them all a penny, which is the parable’s scandal and its comfort (Matthew 20:1). Paul takes the term for himself and his colleagues and adds the astonishing preposition: we are labourers together with God: ye are God’s husbandry, ye are God’s building (1 Corinthians 3:9). And the church’s obligation to support them is stated as a scriptural rule: the labourer is worthy of his reward (1 Timothy 5:18).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LABORER as one who labors in a toilsome occupation; a man who does work that requires little skill, as distinguished from an artisan. Christ’s use of the term for ministers is therefore a deliberate lowering, not an honorific.
webster_full: LABORER, n. — One who labors in a toilsome occupation; a man who does work that requires little skill, as distinguished from an artisan.
One who is employed to perform manual labor for hire; a hireling in the honest sense.
The Authorized Version’s spelling labourer follows the older English orthography which Webster deliberately reformed in his American dictionary.
Matthew 20:1-16 uses the word throughout the parable of the householder and the eleventh hour.
1 Timothy 5:18 joins Deuteronomy 25:4 to a saying of Christ (Luke 10:7) and calls both the scripture — an early and weighty testimony to the canonical status of the Gospels.
scriptures: Matthew 9:37
Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
Matthew 9:38
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.
Matthew 20:1
For the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard.
1 Corinthians 3:9
For we are labourers together with God: ye are God’s husbandry, ye are God’s building.
1 Timothy 5:18
For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward.
corruption_summary: Matthew 9:38 is a command to pray for labourers, and it has been widely replaced by recruitment: conferences, campaigns, and appeals that treat the shortage as a supply problem the church can solve by better marketing.
corruption_paragraphs: The harvest is the Lord’s, the labourers are His to thrust out — the Greek verb is forceful — and the church’s assigned response to a shortage of ministers is prayer. That is not a devotional flourish; it is the only instruction given. Where the call to ministry is treated as a career decision to be encouraged by inspiring events, congregations get men who were persuaded rather than sent, and the Pastoral Epistles’ qualifications become a checklist to be satisfied rather than a description to be recognized. Nothing here forbids training, examination, or ordination councils — all of which Scripture requires. It forbids treating the supply of ministers as anything other than a gift the Lord of the harvest grants in answer to prayer.

Paul’s labourers together with God guards the other flank, against a fatalism that would leave the work undone in the name of sovereignty. The apostle who wrote that God gives the increase and that neither he that planteth nor he that watereth is anything also wrote that he laboured more abundantly than they all, and immediately added, yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me. Both halves are needed. The labourer works with real effort in a field that is not his own, for a harvest he cannot produce, under a Lord who sends and pays. The eleventh-hour men in Matthew 20 received the same penny as the first, which settles once for all that the wage is grace and not calculation.
roots_summary: Greek ergates (G2040), a workman or labourer, from ergon, work; sunergos (G4904), a fellow-worker, in 1 Corinthians 3:9; ekballo (G1544), to thrust forth, in Matthew 9:38.
roots_lines: Greek ergates (G2040) — a labourer, workman; Matthew 9:37-38, 20:1, 1 Timothy 5:18.
Greek ekballo (G1544) — to cast out, to thrust forth; the vigorous verb in send forth labourers.
Greek sunergos (G4904) — a fellow-worker; labourers together with God (1 Corinthians 3:9).
Greek georgion (G1091) — a tilled field, husbandry; ye are God’s husbandry in the same verse.
Greek therismos (G2326) — harvest; the field is his harvest, not the labourers’.
usage: The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few (Matthew 9:37) — the diagnosis, and the prayer that follows it.
We are labourers together with God (1 Corinthians 3:9) — real work in a field that is not ours.
The labourer is worthy of his reward (1 Timothy 5:18) — the church’s duty to those it sends.

etymology: From Latin vomere, to throw up. Webster 1828: matter ejected from the stomach; also, to eject from the stomach. Scripture uses it in two figures of great force — the dog returning to its vomit, and the land itself vomiting out its inhabitants.
biblical_def: Vomit is one of Scripture’s most deliberately repulsive figures, and it is used to describe two things: the false convert and the defiled land. Solomon fixes the first: As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly (Proverbs 26:11). Peter takes the proverb up, adds a second, and applies both to those who had escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of Christ and were entangled again: The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire (2 Peter 2:22). The force of the pairing is exact. Neither animal changed its nature. The dog was reformed of nothing and the sow was washed on the outside; both returned to what they were, and that is Peter’s point about the apostate. The second figure is Leviticus’s, and it is used of the land as a moral agent under God: the land is defiled: therefore I do visit the iniquity thereof upon it, and the land itself vomiteth out her inhabitants (Leviticus 18:25), followed at once by the warning to Israel that it would do the same to her — that the land spue not you out also, when ye defile it, as it spued out the nations that were before you (Leviticus 18:28). The threat was kept in 586 BC.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines VOMIT as matter ejected from the stomach, and as a verb, to eject the contents of the stomach; he cites the scriptural proverb of the dog directly, the phrase having long been current in English.
webster_full: VOMIT, n. — Matter ejected from the stomach; also, an emetic, a medicine that excites vomiting.
VOMIT, v.i. — To eject the contents of the stomach by the mouth.
VOMIT, v.t. — To throw up; to eject from the stomach; and figuratively, to throw out with violence.
The Authorized Version’s spue (Leviticus 18:28; Revelation 3:16) is the older English form of the same idea.
Revelation 3:16 applies the figure to a church rather than a land: because thou art lukewarm… I will spue thee out of my mouth.
scriptures: Proverbs 26:11
As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly.
2 Peter 2:22
But it is happened unto them according to the true proverb, The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire.
Leviticus 18:25
And the land is defiled: therefore I do visit the iniquity thereof upon it, and the land itself vomiteth out her inhabitants.
Leviticus 18:28
That the land spue not you out also, when ye defile it, as it spued out the nations that were before you.
Revelation 3:16
So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
corruption_summary: 2 Peter 2:22 is used on both sides of the perseverance debate; read with its own figures it settles the question, because a dog and a sow that return to type were never anything else.
corruption_paragraphs: The Arminian reading takes the chapter as proof that a saved man may be lost, since these had escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. The figures Peter chose decide it. He does not say the sheep went back to the mire; he says the sow did, after being washed. He does not say a son returned to the vomit; he says the dog did. Washing changed the sow’s outside and not her appetite, and that is precisely the doctrine of regeneration stated from the negative side: what these men lacked was a new nature. John says the same of the same class — they went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us. Peter’s chapter is an argument for the necessity of the new birth, not against the security of the born again.

Leviticus 18 must not be softened either, and it is the passage that shows the conquest was moral rather than tribal. The land is said to vomit out its inhabitants for the abominations catalogued in the chapter — incest, adultery, child sacrifice to Molech, sodomy, and bestiality — and then Israel is told, in the same paragraph, that it will do the same to her for the same things. God did not have a lower standard for His own people. Revelation 3:16 applies the identical figure to a church that had grown comfortable, and the Laodicean sentence is the one the modern Western church should read first: not cold, not hot, and nauseating to Christ for that reason.
roots_summary: Hebrew qi (H6892), vomit, and qo (H6958), to vomit or spue; Greek exerama (G1829), vomit, and emeo (G1692), to spue out, at Revelation 3:16.
roots_lines: Hebrew qo (H6958) — to vomit, to spue out; Leviticus 18:25, 28, and Jonah 2:10 of the fish.
Hebrew qi (H6892) — vomit, the matter itself; Proverbs 26:11, Isaiah 28:8.
Greek exerama (G1829) — vomit; a hapax legomenon at 2 Peter 2:22.
Greek emeo (G1692) — to vomit, to spue; only at Revelation 3:16, of the Laodicean church.
Greek kulisma (G2946) — a wallowing place, a mire; the sow’s return in the same verse.
usage: As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly (Proverbs 26:11) — nature unchanged, behaviour repeating.
The land itself vomiteth out her inhabitants (Leviticus 18:25) — the moral ground of the conquest.
I will spue thee out of my mouth (Revelation 3:16) — the same figure turned on a church.

etymology: From mind and the suffix -ful. Webster 1828: attentive; regarding with care; bearing in mind. In Scripture the word is almost always used of God remembering man or His covenant, which is why its modern career as a technique of self-attention is such a complete inversion.
biblical_def: Mindful in the Authorized Version is nearly always predicated of God, and it carries the whole weight of the psalmist’s astonishment: What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him? (Psalm 8:4). The question is asked while looking at the moon and the stars, and it is not rhetorical self-deprecation; it is a real question about proportion, and Hebrews answers it by applying the psalm to Christ, the Son of man crowned with glory and honour (Hebrews 2:6). The other uses run the same way. He hath given meat unto them that fear him: he will ever be mindful of his covenant (Psalm 111:5) — the ground of confidence is not that we remember the covenant but that He does. The LORD hath been mindful of us: he will bless us (Psalm 115:12). Paul uses it once of himself, in a tender line to Timothy: greatly desiring to see thee, being mindful of thy tears, that I may be filled with joy (2 Timothy 1:4). And Hebrews turns it toward the pilgrims: if they had been mindful of the country whence they came out, they might have returned — but they sought a better country, that is, an heavenly.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MINDFUL as attentive; regarding with care; bearing in mind; heedful; observant. There is no reflexive element in the 1828 definition: to be mindful is to have something else in mind, not to attend to one’s own inner states.
webster_full: MINDFUL, a. — Attentive; regarding with care; bearing in mind; heedful; observant.
The construction is always transitive in older English — mindful of something — and Scripture’s objects are man, the covenant, tears, and a country.
MINDFULNESS was in Webster’s day simply the noun of that adjective: the state of being attentive to something outside oneself.
The modern technical sense of mindfulness, denoting non-judgmental attention to one’s own present experience, enters English from Buddhist sati in the late nineteenth century and is a different word.
Psalm 8:4 is quoted at Hebrews 2:6 and applied to Christ, which fixes the psalm’s ultimate reference.
scriptures: Psalm 8:4
What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?
Hebrews 2:6
But one in a certain place testified, saying, What is man, that thou art mindful of him? or the son of man, that thou visitest him?
Psalm 111:5
He hath given meat unto them that fear him: he will ever be mindful of his covenant.
Psalm 115:12
The LORD hath been mindful of us: he will bless us; he will bless the house of Israel; he will bless the house of Aaron.
2 Timothy 1:4
Greatly desiring to see thee, being mindful of thy tears, that I may be filled with joy;
corruption_summary: Mindfulness in current usage is a therapeutic technique of non-judgmental attention to one’s own experience, imported from Buddhist practice; the biblical word means attention directed outward and upward, and the two have nothing in common but a syllable.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern practice descends from Buddhist sati by way of twentieth-century clinical adaptation, and its governing aim is detached, non-evaluative awareness of the present moment. Every element of that is foreign to Scripture’s vocabulary. Biblical attention is evaluative — prove all things; hold fast that which is good — it is directed away from the self, and its objects are God, His works, His law, and other people. The nearest biblical practice is meditation, and the psalmist’s meditation always has a stated object: I will meditate in thy precepts, I remember the days of old; I meditate on all thy works. A discipline of emptying is not a Christian discipline; the mind in Scripture is filled, renewed, and set on things above.

This is not a reason to despise the ordinary goods that the technique borrows and mislabels. Slowing down, attending to a single thing, and refusing anxious rumination are all commended in Scripture, and the Lord commanded the consideration of lilies and birds against exactly the anxiety that fills a modern mind. But the reason He gave was doctrinal, not psychological: your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they? The cure for a racing mind in Scripture is not attention to attention. It is Psalm 8 — look at the moon and the stars, ask what man is, and find that the God who made them is mindful of you.
roots_summary: Hebrew zakar (H2142), to remember, to be mindful of; Greek mimnesko (G3403), to remember, and phroneo-family words for the mind’s set.
roots_lines: Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember, to bring to mind, to be mindful; Psalm 8:4, 111:5, 115:12.
Greek mimnesko (G3403) — to remind, to be mindful of; Hebrews 2:6 and 2 Timothy 1:4.
Greek phroneo (G5426) — to set the mind on; set your affection on things above (Colossians 3:2).
Greek meletao (G3191) — to meditate, to attend carefully to; meditate upon these things (1 Timothy 4:15).
Hebrew hagah (H1897) — to muse, to mutter, to meditate; the verb of Psalm 1:2, meditation with an object.
usage: What is man, that thou art mindful of him? (Psalm 8:4) — the question asked under the stars.
He will ever be mindful of his covenant (Psalm 111:5) — the ground of assurance is His memory, not ours.
Being mindful of thy tears (2 Timothy 1:4) — an apostle’s attention fixed on someone else.

etymology: From the older English quite, to acquit or pay off, with the intensive prefix re-; the same root as quit and acquittance. Webster 1828: to repay; to return an equivalent in good or evil. Scripture uses it of children repaying parents, of God repaying His enemies, and of Israel’s shameful repayment of her Father.
biblical_def: Requite means to pay back, and Scripture uses it in three directions. The first is filial: if any widow have children or nephews, let them learn first to shew piety at home, and to requite their parents: for that is good and acceptable before God (1 Timothy 5:4). Paul makes the care of an aged mother a debt owed, not a kindness offered, and calls the failure of it worse than infidelity three verses later. The second is God’s: the LORD God of recompences shall surely requite (Jeremiah 51:56), spoken over Babylon, and it is the ground on which Christians are forbidden private vengeance — avenge not yourselves… Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord. The third is the most searching. Moses turns the word on Israel in the song he taught them before he died: Do ye thus requite the LORD, O foolish people and unwise? is not he thy father that hath bought thee? hath he not made thee, and established thee? (Deuteronomy 32:6). Three claims — He made you, bought you, established you — and the question is what you have paid Him back. Joseph’s brothers assumed he would requite them all the evil they had done, and he wept and did the opposite.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines REQUITE as to repay; to make return; to return an equivalent in good or evil, and notes that the return may be of kindness or of injury — a neutrality Scripture’s usage shares exactly.
webster_full: REQUITE, v.t. — To repay; to return an equivalent in good or evil; to recompense.
To repay with good; to reward; as, I also will requite you this kindness (2 Samuel 2:6).
To repay with evil; to retaliate; as, will certainly requite us all the evil which we did unto him (Genesis 50:15).
From the obsolete verb quite, to acquit or discharge a debt, whence also quit, quittance, and acquittance.
The debt language is not accidental: to requite is to settle an account, which is why 1 Timothy 5:4 can make it a duty rather than a sentiment.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 5:4
But if any widow have children or nephews, let them learn first to shew piety at home, and to requite their parents: for that is good and acceptable before God.
Deuteronomy 32:6
Do ye thus requite the LORD, O foolish people and unwise? is not he thy father that hath bought thee? hath he not made thee, and established thee?
2 Samuel 2:6
And now the LORD shew kindness and truth unto you: and I also will requite you this kindness, because ye have done this thing.
Jeremiah 51:56
Because the spoiler is come upon her, even upon Babylon, and her mighty men are taken, every one of their bows is broken: for the LORD God of recompences shall surely requite.
Romans 12:19
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
corruption_summary: 1 Timothy 5:4 makes the care of aged parents a debt to be discharged by their own children first, and the modern reflex — that this is what the state or the institution is for — is a straightforward abandonment of the fifth commandment.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul’s instruction about widows is one of the most concrete pieces of social teaching in the New Testament, and its logic runs opposite to the modern assumption. The children and grandchildren are to requite their parents first; the church supports the widow who is a widow indeed, and desolate, meaning she has no family left; and the man who does not provide for his own house hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel. The sequence is family, then church, and the state does not appear. Where care is outsourced by default while children live within reach, a debt is being left unpaid, and Paul’s word for the paying of it is piety — the same reverence owed to God, shown at home. Our Lord condemned the Corban evasion on exactly this ground.

Romans 12:19 supplies the other side, and it is more comfort than restraint. The believer is forbidden to requite evil not because the evil does not matter but because the LORD God of recompences shall surely requite, and He will do it justly, which no private man can. The prohibition of vengeance in Scripture always rests on the certainty of judgment, never on its denial; a God who would let it go would leave the injured with nothing but their own hands. This also leaves the civil magistrate exactly where Romans 13 puts him in the very next paragraph — a minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil. Private vengeance is forbidden; public justice is God’s ordinance.
roots_summary: Hebrew gamal (H1580), to deal out, to recompense, in Deuteronomy 32:6; shalam (H7999), to make whole, to repay, in Jeremiah 51:56; Greek amoibe (G287), a return or recompense, in 1 Timothy 5:4.
roots_lines: Hebrew gamal (H1580) — to deal out to, to recompense, to wean; do ye thus requite the LORD? (Deuteronomy 32:6).
Hebrew shalam (H7999) — to be complete, to make good, to repay; the root of shalom and of restitution law.
Greek amoibe (G287) — a requital, a return; a hapax legomenon at 1 Timothy 5:4.
Greek ekdikesis (G1557) — vengeance, the full execution of justice; vengeance is mine (Romans 12:19).
Greek eusebeo (G2151) — to show piety toward; the verb Paul uses of a child’s duty to a parent in the same verse.
usage: To requite their parents: for that is good and acceptable before God (1 Timothy 5:4) — care of the aged as a debt.
Do ye thus requite the LORD, O foolish people and unwise? (Deuteronomy 32:6) — the question of Moses’ song.
The LORD God of recompences shall surely requite (Jeremiah 51:56) — why private vengeance is forbidden.
